lessons.title: Study Session 1: Naming What You're Actually Building Toward

blocks.text: Introduction

Fatima Osman had a vague sense that she wanted to grow in her career, but no answer when a mentor asked her, plainly, grow into what, exactly, and by when. This session teaches you to turn that vague sense into a specific, workable goal, so your career planning has something real to aim at.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
e Explain why a specific, challenging goal produces better results than a vague intention to improve. e Distinguish a goal from a general hope or wish.
¢ Connect a career goal to her own actual values, not borrowed ambitions.
e Set one specific, time-bound career goal for the coming year.
e Identify the feedback she will use to know whether she is making progress. 2.0 Main Content
A Vague Answer to a Direct Question

Fatima Osman manages a customer accounts team at a telecommunications firm in Khartoum, and when a mentor at a professional women's network asked her where she wanted to be in three years, she answered honestly: somewhere better than here. The mentor did not accept it as an answer. She asked Fatima to try again, this time with a role, a skill, or a number attached.
Why Specific Goals Outperform Vague Ones

In 1990, the researchers Edwin Locke and Gary Latham published A Theory of Goal Setting and Task Performance, drawing together decades of studies on what actually motivates sustained effort and improved performance. Their central finding, replicated across hundreds of studies, is direct: specific, challenging goals produce significantly better performance than vague goals such as do your best, because a specific goal gives a person something concrete to measure progress against and a clear point at which effort can be judged to have succeeded.
Turning a Vague Sense Into a Real Goal

Naming a Specific Outcome, Not a General Direction A goal stated as become a senior accounts manager by the end of next year gives Fatima something to plan toward; a goal stated as grow professionally gives her nothing she can act on differently tomorrow.
Checking the Goal Against Her Own Values

A goal borrowed from what looks impressive to others, rather than connected to what Fatima actually values, tends to lose its pull the moment the work required for it gets difficult; naming why a goal matters to her personally makes it far more likely to survive a hard month.
Naming the Feedback That Will Tell Her She Is on Track

A goal without a way to measure progress leaves a person unable to tell whether she is moving toward it or only feeling busy; naming, in advance, what evidence would show real progress turns a vague sense of effort into something she can actually check.
Key Practices

e State your goal as a specific outcome, not a general direction. e Connect your goal to what you actually value, not what looks impressive to others. e Set areal deadline, even an imperfect one, rather than leaving a goal open ended. e Name the specific feedback or evidence that will tell you whether you are making progress.
e Revisit your stated goal often enough that it stays real, not filed away and forgotten.
A Worked Example: Fatima's Goal, Named

After her mentor's question, Fatima named her actual goal: become a senior accounts manager within eighteen months, by leading at least one cross-department project and completing a recognised customer relationship management certification. She connected it to something she genuinely valued, the chance to shape how her team treated struggling customers, rather than simply a bigger title.

She also named her evidence in advance: a completed certification, a completed cross-department project with documented outcomes, and a formal conversation with her current manager about readiness for the next role. Eight months in, she could point to two of the three and knew exactly what remained.
Common Pitfalls

Stating a goal in terms so broad it could mean almost anything, grow, improve, do better, is the trap that catches most people at the start of career planning, because a goal that broad offers nothing to actually plan around and nothing concrete to measure later. A goal a person cannot fail is usually a goal too vague to have actually motivated anything.
A Target Worth Aiming At

Fatima's career plan did not become more ambitious the day she named her goal specifically. It became usable, because for the first time she had something concrete enough to actually plan a year around.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion
In this study session, you learned to turn a vague sense of ambition into a specific, values-connected goal with
clear feedback for measuring progress. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where you will map the wider path that goal actually sits on.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. State one career goal you currently hold in a single, specific, time-bound sentence.
2. Name one piece of evidence that would tell you, six months from now, whether you are actually making progress toward that goal. Practical Output: Practical Output
One written, specific career goal with a deadline, a connection to a personal value, and named evidence of progress.
References and Further Reading
e Locke, E.A., & Latham, G.P. (1990). A Theory of Goal Setting and Task Performance. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Prentice Hall.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 21:5, on the plans of the diligent leading surely to abundance.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Qasas 28:77, on seeking one's share of this world through what Allah has given, without forgetting the greater purpose.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Seeing the Path, Not Just the Next Step

blocks.text: Introduction

Lea Nguema had only ever thought about her career one promotion at a time, never the shape of the whole road ahead. This session teaches you to map a career path across its real stages, so a single next step stops being the only thing you can see.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Explain why career development unfolds across recognisable life stages rather than a single fixed ladder. e Identify which stage of career development she is currently in. e Map at least two realistic route options beyond her current role.
¢ Distinguish a role that fits her current stage from one that fits a different stage entirely. 2.0 Main Content
One Step at a Time, With No Map

Lea Nguema works as a quality control officer at a beverage manufacturing plant in Libreville, and for six years she had planned her career exactly one step ahead, the next available promotion, whatever it happened to be, without ever asking whether it led anywhere she actually wanted to go. When a shift supervisor role opened, she nearly took it out of habit, before a colleague asked her a simple question: did she actually want to manage shifts, or did she just want to move.
A Career Unfolds in Stages, Not a Straight Line

In 1980, the psychologist Donald Super published A Life-Span, Life-Space Approach to Career Development in the Journal of Vocational Behavior, describing career development as a series of recognisable life stages, growth, exploration, establishment, maintenance and decline, rather than a single fixed ladder climbed the same way by everyone. His finding was that a person's priorities and the kind of role that actually fits her shift across these stages, meaning a role that suited her five years ago may no longer fit where she is now, and a role that looks like progress on paper may not match her actual current stage at all.
Mapping the Road, Not Just the Next Step

Naming Her Current Stage Honestly Recognising whether she is still exploring what fits her, establishing herself in a chosen direction, or maintaining and deepening expertise already built, shapes which opportunities are actually worth pursuing right now.

Sketching More Than One Route Forward Naming two or three realistic paths beyond her current role, not just the single most obvious promotion, reveals options a person locked onto one path never considers.
Testing Whether an Opportunity Fits the Stage She Is Actually In

An opportunity that would suit someone in a different stage, a person still exploring taking a role built for someone ready to specialise deeply, or the reverse, often looks like progress while actually working against where a person genuinely is.
Key Practices

e Name your current career stage honestly before evaluating an opportunity. e Map at least two realistic routes forward, not only the single most obvious one. e Test whether an opportunity actually fits your current stage, not just its job title.
e Revisit your career map periodically, since your stage will shift over time.
A Worked Example: Lea's Two Routes

Once Lea named her stage honestly, still establishing her expertise in quality systems rather than ready to manage people, the shift supervisor role looked different. It would have moved her into people management before she had finished building the technical depth she actually wanted.

She mapped two alternative routes instead: a senior quality analyst role that deepened her technical expertise, and a longer-term path toward quality systems consulting that used that same expertise across multiple sites. She chose to pursue the senior analyst role first, not because it was the only option, but because it matched the stage she was actually in.
Common Pitfalls

Accepting the next available promotion simply because it appears next, without checking whether it actually fits her current stage or chosen direction, traps many careful workers into a role that looks like progress but quietly moves them away from what they actually wanted. A step upward is not automatically a step forward.
A Road With More Than One Turn

Lea's career plan did not become slower once she stopped taking whatever step appeared next. It became a road with an actual shape, one she could see several turns ahead instead of only the one directly in front of her.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to map your career across recognisable stages and more than one realistic route, rather than reacting to whichever step appears next. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where you will identify the specific skill gaps that stand between you and the path you have mapped.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Which career stage, growth, exploration, establishment, maintenance or decline, best describes where you are right now?
2. Name two realistic routes forward from your current role, not just the most obvious next step. Practical Output: Practical Output
A simple map naming her current career stage and two realistic routes forward, with one sentence on why each route does or does not fit her stage.
References and Further Reading
e Super, D.E. (1980). A life-span, life-space approach to career development. Journal of Vocational Behavior, 16, 282 to 298.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 4:26, on pondering the path of your feet so all your ways may be sure.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-An'am 6:135, on working according to one's own position and situation.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Closing the Gap Between Here and There

blocks.text: Introduction

Delphine Mbarga knew exactly what skill stood between her and the role she wanted, and still spent a year improving barely at all, practising the same way, in the same scattered moments, between caring for her young son and finishing her own workday. This session teaches you to close a skill gap through deliberate, structured practice, not just repeated exposure.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
¢ Distinguish a skill gap from a general feeling of not being ready.
e Explain why repeated exposure to a task does not reliably improve skill on its own. e Identify the specific, narrow skill that most limits her progress right now.
e Design one piece of deliberate practice targeting that specific skill.
e Build feedback into her practice so she knows whether it is actually working.
e Fit meaningful practice into a realistically limited amount of time. 2.0 Main Content
A Year of Practice That Barely Moved the Needle

Delphine Mbarga works as a translator for an international organisation in Yaounde, and for over a year she believed that simply translating more documents would sharpen the specific skill she actually needed, rendering technical legal language clearly for a general audience. She translated a great deal in that year. Her manager's feedback on that particular skill barely changed.
Practice Alone Is Not Enough

In 1993, the researchers Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Romer published a study in Psychological Review examining what actually separated expert performers from experienced but merely average ones across several fields. Their finding reshaped how skill development is understood: raw years of experience or repeated exposure to a task does not reliably predict expertise. What predicts it is deliberate practice, effortful, structured practice specifically targeted at a person's actual weakness, with clear feedback, performed consistently over time, not simply doing more of what a person already does comfortably.
Practising the One Thing That Actually Limits Her
Naming the Actual Narrow Skill

A general feeling of not being ready is not a skill gap; naming the one specific, narrow capability that most limits current progress, rendering technical language plainly rather than translation in general, turns a vague anxiety into something practice can actually target.
Designing Practice Around That Specific Gap

Practice that targets the named gap directly, deliberately rewriting a dense legal passage into plain language and comparing it against a strong model, builds the specific skill faster than simply doing more of the broader task surrounding it.
Building In Feedback That Tells Her Whether It Is Working

Practice without feedback repeats the same mistakes indefinitely; asking a colleague or mentor to review targeted practice attempts, or comparing them against a known strong example, is what turns effort into actual improvement.
Key Practices

e Name the one specific, narrow skill that most limits your current progress. ¢ Design practice that targets that exact gap, not the broader task around it. e Build in feedback so you know whether your practice is actually working. e Practise in short, consistent sessions that fit realistically into a limited schedule.
e Track improvement on the specific skill, not only general output.
A Worked Example: Delphine's Deliberate Practice

Once Delphine named the actual gap, plain-language rendering of technical legal terms, she stopped translating more documents in general and started a narrower practice instead: twenty minutes, three evenings a week after her son was asleep, rewriting one dense legal paragraph into plain language, then comparing her version against a model produced by a senior colleague.

She asked that same colleague to review one practice attempt every two weeks. Within two months, feedback on her actual translations at work began noting the exact improvement she had been practising toward. The change had nothing to do with translating more. It came from practising the one narrow thing that had actually been limiting her.
Common Pitfalls

Mistaking general repetition for deliberate improvement is the error that quietly wastes the most effort at this stage, because doing more of a broad task feels productive while rarely targeting the specific, narrow skill that is actually holding a person back. Effort spent without a clear target or feedback loop often produces very little real change, however much time it consumes.
Small, Targeted, and Real

Delphine's practice sessions were short and specific, not exhausting marathons of extra work stacked onto an already full day. What made them effective was not their length. It was that every minute of them was aimed at the exact thing she actually needed to improve.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to name a specific skill gap and close it through deliberate, feedback-driven practice, rather than general repetition. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where mentorship becomes a source of exactly the feedback this kind of practice depends on.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Name one specific, narrow skill, not a general area, that currently limits your progress toward a career goal.
2. Design one short, realistic practice session you could fit into your week to target that specific skill. Practical Output: Practical Output
One deliberate practice plan naming a specific skill gap, a targeted practice activity, a feedback source, and a realistic weekly time commitment.
References and Further Reading

e Ericsson, K.A., Krampe, R.Th., & Tesch-Romer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100, 363 to 406. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Ecclesiastes 10:10, on a blunt iron requiring more strength, when wisdom helps one to succeed.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Ankabut 29:69, on those who strive being guided in their ways.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Finding Someone Who's Already Walked This Road

blocks.text: Introduction

Aicha Moussa assumed a mentor's only job was to give career advice occasionally over coffee, until a real mentoring relationship taught her that the most useful support she received was rarely advice at all. This session teaches you to seek out and use mentorship deliberately, for both the career guidance and the quieter support it can actually offer.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Distinguish career-focused mentoring functions from psychosocial mentoring functions. e Identify what she actually needs from a mentoring relationship right now. e Approach a potential mentor with a specific, low-pressure request.
e Sustain a mentoring relationship by contributing to it, not only drawing from it. 2.0 Main Content
A Mentor Who Rarely Gave Advice

Aicha Moussa works as a project officer for a regional development agency in N'Djamena, and when a senior colleague agreed to mentor her, Aicha expected regular sessions of direct career advice. What she actually received, most months, was something quieter: a senior colleague who listened without judgement after a difficult meeting, who mentioned her name in rooms she was not in, and who modelled, simply by how she carried herself, what confidence under pressure could look like.
Mentoring Does Two Different Kinds of Work

In 1985, the researcher Kathy Kram published Mentoring at Work, based on a close study of developmental relationships inside organisations, distinguishing two distinct functions a mentor provides. Career functions include sponsorship, exposure to opportunities, and coaching, direct support for advancement. Psychosocial functions include acceptance, confirmation, counsel and friendship, support for a person's confidence and professional identity. Kram's central finding was that both functions matter, and a mentoring relationship that offers only one, direct advice with no genuine support, or warmth with no real career exposure, is incomplete.
Approaching and Sustaining Mentorship on Purpose
Naming What She Actually Needs Right Now

Being specific about whether she currently needs career-focused support, exposure to new opportunities, coaching on a skill, or psychosocial support, confidence, perspective, encouragement, helps her approach the right kind of relationship rather than a vague, undefined one.

Making a Low-Pressure, Specific Request Asking a potential mentor for one small, defined thing, thirty minutes to discuss a specific decision, rather than an open-ended, ongoing commitment, makes it far easier for a busy senior colleague to say yes.

Contributing to the Relationship, Not Only Drawing From It A mentoring relationship that only takes from a mentor's time and goodwill tends to fade; sharing something useful in return, a relevant contact, a piece of information, simple genuine appreciation, helps sustain it.
Key Practices

e Distinguish whether you currently need career-focused support or psychosocial support, or both. e Approach a potential mentor with one small, specific, low-pressure request. e Notice and value the quieter psychosocial support a mentor offers, not only direct advice.
¢ Contribute something back to a mentoring relationship rather than only drawing from it.
A Worked Example: Aicha's Two Requests

Aicha's first request to her senior colleague was specific and small: thirty minutes to review how she had handled a difficult donor meeting. That single conversation became the beginning of an ongoing relationship, not because Aicha asked for an ongoing relationship, but because the first request was easy to say yes to.

Months later, recognising she now needed a different kind of support, exposure to a wider network ahead of a coming role change, Aicha made a second, equally specific request: an introduction to two contacts in a partner organisation. She also began sending her mentor relevant articles and, when she moved into a position to do so, offered informal support of her own to a newer colleague, understanding that mentoring relationships are sustained by more than one person always taking.
Common Pitfalls

Expecting a mentor to provide only direct career advice, and overlooking or undervaluing the quieter psychosocial support offered alongside it, causes many people to underestimate a mentoring relationship that is actually working well in a different way than they expected. A mentor who never hands out explicit advice may still be doing some of the most valuable work of the relationship.
A Relationship, Not a Transaction

Aicha's mentoring relationship has lasted years, not because either of them formalised it heavily, but because it has always involved something moving in both directions, specific requests met with specific help, and quieter support offered and, eventually, returned.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to seek mentorship deliberately, recognising both its career and psychosocial functions, and to sustain it by contributing as well as receiving. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where the same honest self-awareness shapes how you balance career ambition against the rest of your life.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Do you currently need more career-focused support or psychosocial support from a mentor, or both? Name specifically what that support would look like.
2. Name one small, specific request you could make of a potential mentor this month. Practical Output: Practical Output
One specific, low-pressure request drafted for a real or potential mentor, naming exactly what kind of support is being asked for.
References and Further Reading
e Kram, K.E. (1985). Mentoring at Work: Developmental Relationships in Organizational Life. Glenview, IL: Scott, Foresman and Company.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 27:9, on the sweetness of a friend's earnest counsel.
e Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:66, on Musa asking to follow and learn from one given greater knowledge.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: A Plan That Fits a Whole Life

blocks.text: Introduction

Salamata Ouedraogo, raising two children alone in Ouagadougou, learned the hard way that a career plan built as though she had unlimited time and energy would eventually cost her both. This session teaches you to plan a career that respects the actual, limited resources of a whole life, not just the working hours inside it.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Explain why people protect and invest limited resources rather than treating time and energy as unlimited. e Identify which resources, time, energy, support, are most under strain in her own life right now.
e Distinguish a career investment worth a real resource cost from one that is not.
e Build one realistic adjustment that protects a strained resource without abandoning her career goal.
e Recognise early signs that her resources are becoming dangerously depleted. 2.0 Main Content
A Certification Pursued at the Wrong Cost

Salamata Ouedraogo works in accounts for a construction firm in Ouagadougou and raises her two children alone, and she enrolled in an evening certification programme believing it would only cost her a few hours a week. Within two months, she was skipping meals to find study time, her children were going to bed later than she wanted, and she was exhausted at work in ways that were beginning to show. The certification was not the problem. The plan around it had never accounted for what she actually had left to spend.
People Protect What They Cannot Easily Replace

In 1989, the psychologist Stevan Hobfoll published Conservation of Resources in American Psychologist, describing a model of stress built on a simple premise: people work to protect, retain and build valued resources, time, energy, social support, a sense of control, and experience genuine strain when those resources are threatened or lost faster than they can be replaced. His finding was that sustainable effort depends on managing a real, limited resource pool, not on willpower alone, and that a plan which spends down resources faster than it replenishes them will eventually fail, regardless of how worthwhile its goal is.
Planning Around Real, Limited Resources
Naming Which Resource Is Actually Under Strain

Identifying honestly whether time, energy, social support or a sense of control is the resource actually running short, rather than assuming the problem is simply insufficient effort, points toward a solution that might actually work.
Weighing a Career Investment Against Its Real Cost

A career opportunity worth pursuing in principle can still be the wrong choice at a given moment if its actual resource cost, in time, energy or strain on caregiving responsibilities, exceeds what a person genuinely has to spend right now.
Building a Small Adjustment That Protects the Strained Resource

A single realistic change, moving study time to a period that does not compete with a child's bedtime, asking a relative for two hours of support once a week, can protect a limited resource without requiring the larger goal to be abandoned.
Key Practices

e Name honestly which resource, time, energy or support, is actually under the most strain. e Weigh a career opportunity against its real cost to your current resources, not only its future benefit. ¢ Build one small, realistic adjustment that protects a strained resource.
e Watch for early signs of resource depletion, exhaustion, skipped meals, strained relationships, before they become severe.
e Ask for support explicitly rather than assuming none is available.
A Worked Example: Salamata's Adjustment

Salamata named her actual strained resource honestly: not motivation, but time and energy, spent entirely without any additional support. She did not abandon her certification. She moved her study sessions to two mornings a week before her children woke, arranged with her sister for two hours of help on Saturday afternoons, and cut her course load from two modules at once to one.

The certification took four months longer to finish. She finished it without the exhaustion and skipped meals that had marked her first two months, and her children's bedtime routine returned to what it had been before she started.
Common Pitfalls

Treating time and energy as though they were unlimited, and adding a new career commitment on top of an already full life without adjusting anything else, is the assumption that quietly damages both careers and wellbeing at this stage. A worthwhile goal pursued at an unsustainable resource cost often collapses entirely, achieving less than a slower, better-supported pace would have.
A Plan Built to Actually Last
Salamata's certification goal did not change. What changed was a plan that finally accounted for the whole life it had to fit inside, rather than assuming that life would simply make room.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to plan a career goal around your real, limited resources of time, energy and support, rather than assuming they are unlimited. This prepares you for Study Session 6, where you will review and adjust your whole career plan as your circumstances continue to change.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Which resource, time, energy, social support or a sense of control, is under the most strain in your life right now?
2. Name one small, realistic adjustment you could make to protect that resource without abandoning a current career goal. Practical Output: Practical Output
Awritten plan naming her most strained resource, one real adjustment to protect it, and one source of support she will explicitly ask for. 7.0 References and Further Reading
e Hobfoll, S.E. (1989). Conservation of resources: A new attempt at conceptualizing stress. American Psychologist, 44, 513 to 524.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Ecclesiastes 4:6, on a handful of quietness being better than two hands full of toil.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Bagarah 2:286, on Allah not charging a soul beyond its capacity.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.
Introduction

Every session so far has built one part of a career plan. This final session asks Voahangy Razafy, and you, to step back and review the whole plan honestly, using what has actually happened so far, not just what was originally hoped, to decide what comes next.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Review a career plan against what has actually happened since it was made. e Explain how small, real successes build the confidence to attempt larger ones. e Revise a goal, route or practice plan based on real evidence rather than starting over from scratch.
¢ Commit to a specific date for the plan's next honest review. 2.0 Main Content
A Plan Left Untouched for a Year

Voahangy Razafy coordinates monitoring and evaluation for an agricultural cooperative network in Antananarivo, and she had written a thorough career plan a year earlier, then filed it away and never looked at it again. When a colleague asked how the plan was going, Voahangy realised she could not actually say, because she had never gone back to check it against what had actually happened in the year since.
Confidence Is Built From Real Evidence

In 1977, the psychologist Albert Bandura published Self-Efficacy: Toward a Unifying Theory of Behavioral Change in Psychological Review, describing how a person's belief in her own ability to succeed at a specific task, her self- efficacy, is built most powerfully through direct evidence of her own past success, more than through encouragement or comparison with others. His finding matters directly for career planning: reviewing a plan honestly, naming what has actually been achieved so far, however small, builds the real confidence needed to take on the next, larger step, while a plan never reviewed offers no such evidence at all.
Reviewing and Revising Honestly
Checking the Plan Against What Actually Happened

Reading a career plan again after real time has passed, and comparing it honestly against what was actually done, reveals both real progress worth recognising and gaps worth addressing directly, neither of which a filed-away plan can show on its own.
Naming Small Real Successes as Evidence

Explicitly naming what has actually been achieved, a certification finished, a mentoring relationship built, a skill measurably improved, builds genuine confidence for the next stage, because it is evidence, not simply encouragement.
Revising Rather Than Restarting

A plan that has partly succeeded and partly stalled usually needs specific adjustment, a goal reworded, a route reconsidered, a resource reprotected, rather than being abandoned and rewritten from nothing, which discards real progress already made.
Key Practices

e Set a specific date to review your career plan, and keep it. ¢ Compare the plan honestly against what has actually happened since it was made. e Name small real successes explicitly as evidence, not just as things to feel good about briefly. e Revise specific parts of a stalled plan rather than discarding the whole thing.
¢ Carry the revised plan forward with a new review date already set.
A Worked Example: Voahangy's Honest Review

When Voahangy finally reread her year-old plan, she found real progress in one area, she had built the mentoring relationship she had named as a goal, and real stalling in another, the technical certification she had planned to complete had not been started at all, for reasons that turned out to be a genuine, unaddressed resource strain similar to Salamata's.

Rather than rewriting her entire plan, she named the mentoring relationship explicitly as real evidence of what she could achieve when she planned deliberately, and revised only the stalled certification goal, adjusting its timeline and building in the resource protection Session 5 had taught. She set her next review date for six months out, in her calendar, not left to memory.
Common Pitfalls

Filing a career plan away and never returning to it, treating the act of writing it as though it were the whole task, is the mistake that quietly undoes even careful planning at this final stage. A plan that is never reviewed cannot tell a person what actually worked, what stalled, or what confidence she has genuinely earned to build on.
A Plan That Keeps Working

Voahangy's career plan is no longer a document written once and left untouched. It is something she returns to ona set date, honestly, using what has actually happened as evidence for what comes next, which is the habit this entire course has been building toward.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to review a career plan honestly against real evidence, revise it specifically rather than restarting it, and set a date to return to it again. This closes Course 81 and prepares you for Course 82, Mentorship and Professional Networks.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. If you wrote a career plan today, what date would you set to review it honestly?
2. Name one small real success from the past year that could serve as genuine evidence of what you are capable of achieving. Practical Output: Practical Output
One honest review of an existing career goal or plan, naming real progress, one stalled element with its cause,
and a specific date for the next review.
